1991 · statutory arrangement letting the government direct the bank. Aruba's Central Bank Ordinance (AB 1991 no. GT 32), as amended through AB 2014 no. 5 and published by the Centrale Bank van Aruba in Dutch and in the bank's English translation, keeps the bank under the Governor of Aruba and the Minister of Finance. Section 18 says the president and executive directors are appointed by the Governor from a shortlist of three put up by the Supervisory Board, and that the Governor may suspend or dismiss them by state decree. Section 19(3) says general guidelines for the performance of the duties of the president and executive directors can be set out in a state decree. Section 23 says the chairman of the Supervisory Board is the Government Commissioner, appointed and dismissed by the Governor, that the other supervisory directors are appointed by the Governor, and that they may be suspended or dismissed before the end of their term by the Governor. Section 27(1) says the Government Commissioner supervises the bank's activities on behalf of the Country and acts in accordance with general or specific instructions given by the Minister. This is a standing arrangement with no end date. Central Bank Ordinance (AB 1991 no. GT 32), English translation (Centrale Bank van Aruba)

BERMUDA MONETARY AUTHORITY
Bermuda
Bermuda's money is the Bermudian dollar, issued by the Bermuda Monetary Authority, which is the central bank. As of December 2025 the dollar sat in a de facto peg to the US dollar, meaning it is held at a fixed rate in practice. Independence written into law is almost absent, 0.06 of 1 and second from last of 191 places, with no reform since 1970, and the bank scores 3.5 of 15 for what it tells the public. Bermuda scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; the weakest part is corruption and secrecy around the bank, at 50, mainly because the island's laws hide who owns money, with financial secrecy at 71.3 of 100, 54th of 141 places. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. One career move is recorded: Cheryl-Ann Lister, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the Authority from 1999 through 2006, was appointed an independent director and audit committee member of AXIS Capital Holdings Limited, a Bermuda-based insurance and reinsurance group, in an announcement of 23 September 2008. The Office of the Auditor-General audits the accounts, as it did for 2021. The notes are printed abroad: the authority announced on 30 October 2024 that its new 2 and 5 dollar notes, printed by De La Rue on polymer, would enter circulation that autumn, Bermuda's first polymer notes and among the first anywhere to carry King Charles III's effigy.

CENTRAL BANK OF BARBADOS
Barbados
The Central Bank of Barbados issues the Barbados dollar and in practice holds it at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. In 2017 Finance Minister Chris Sinckler dismissed Governor Delisle Worrell. The government's stated reason was that the board objected to his reported high-handed manner; some observers believed the reason was his refusal to keep financing the government with new money, which he had set out in a letter that January saying the government must stop taking new money from the bank to pay its bills. The Appeals Court upheld the minister's right to dismiss him. Apart from that, no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. The bank's founding governor, Sir Courtney Blackman, had been an economist at the Wall Street bank Irving Trust Company from 1968 to 1971, led the bank from 1972 to 1987 across three terms while also serving as Barbados' alternate governor to the International Monetary Fund until March 1987, and from 1987 to 1994 worked as an international business consultant and as director general of corporations and financial institutions that the bank's own page does not name. Its five-dollar polymer note, introduced in December 2022, is printed by De La Rue. Barbados scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and the bank tells the public little, 3 of 15 on a transparency measure. The bank's accounts are audited by PricewaterhouseCoopers SRL of Bridgetown, whose report for the year ended 31 December 2025 is dated 27 March 2026.

The Auditor General's 2021 report found that cheques totalling $10,198,548.08 recorded on Treasury cashiers' reports for 22 September 2020 did not agree with the Central Bank of Barbados listing, which recorded $3,536,006.77, a difference of $6,662,541.31 for which no explanation was given. 2018-2019 · unexplained accounts or weak controls · official finding. The Auditor General's 2020 report found that bank reconciliations for Treasury accounts at the Central Bank of Barbados were not completed up to 31 March 2019, and that the Central Bank account had last been reconciled in May 2018. The report noted that monthly reconciliation is an internal control that can detect fraud or errors. Report of the Auditor General for the year 2020 (Barbados Audit Office)

The Auditor General's 2020 report examined 29 transactions in which the Accountant General authorises the Central Bank of Barbados by signed memorandum to transfer loan funds to lending agencies. p:BRB.current_paragraph: The Central Bank of Barbados issues the Barbados dollar and in practice holds it at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. In 2017 Finance Minister Chris Sinckler dismissed Governor Delisle Worrell. The government's stated reason was that the board objected to his reported high-handed manner; some observers believed the reason was his refusal to keep financing the government with new money, which he had set out in a letter that January saying the government must stop taking new money from the bank to pay its bills. The Appeals Court upheld the minister's right to dismiss him. Apart from that, no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. The bank's founding governor, Sir Courtney Blackman, had been an economist at the Wall Street bank Irving Trust Company from 1968 to 1971, led the bank from 1972 to 1987 across three terms while also serving as Barbados' alternate governor to the International Monetary Fund until March 1987, and from 1987 to 1994 worked as an international business consultant and as director general of corporations and financial institutions that the bank's own page does not name. Its five-dollar polymer note, introduced in December 2022, is printed by De La Rue. Barbados scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and the bank tells the public little, 3 of 15 on a transparency measure. The bank's accounts are audited by PricewaterhouseCoopers SRL of Bridgetown, whose report for the year ended 31 December 2025 is dated 27 March 2026.

Chile
Chile's central bank is the Central Bank of Chile, which issues the Chilean peso. The Constitutional Convention elected to write a replacement for the 1980 constitution drafted new articles on the bank, and on 5 April 2022 its president Rosanna Costa wrote to the Convention on the Council's behalf setting out what it objected to. The main objection was the removal provision: one third of the members of Congress could have asked the Supreme Court to remove councillors, which the bank said exposed it to political judgements that would diminish its autonomy and its working. CENTRAL BANK OF THE COMOROS
Comoros
The Central Bank of the Comoros issues the Comorian franc, and France stands behind it. A monetary cooperation agreement signed at Moroni and Paris on 23 November 1979 rests on an unlimited French guarantee of the currency the bank issues. That agreement set the rate at 1 Comorian franc to 0.02 French francs; after a devaluation of 33 percent on 11 January 1994, the rate is now 1 euro to 491.968 Comorian francs. The bank must keep 65 percent of its foreign currency reserves on deposit with the French Treasury. Two governments also fill its board. Under statutes signed in Paris on 22 April 2008 it had at most eight members, half named by the French government and half by the government of the Union of the Comoros, with the Governor named by the President of the Union on the finance minister's proposal; the board approved a new draft on 28 June 2024 that still awaited promulgation at the end of 2024. Under statutes in force since March 2025, France names two of the six board members, two of the four members of the banking supervision committee and two of the four members of the committee that sets monetary policy and manages reserves. The notes are printed at the Banque de France, and a new 10,000-franc note was reportedly introduced on 6 January 2026. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. It holds no gold, Mazars Fivoarana audited its 2024 accounts, and it scores 65 of 100, the highest of the 194 places with a figure.

p:COM.current_paragraph: The Central Bank of the Comoros issues the Comorian franc, and France stands behind it. A monetary cooperation agreement signed at Moroni and Paris on 23 November 1979 rests on an unlimited French guarantee of the currency the bank issues. That agreement set the rate at 1 Comorian franc to 0.02 French francs; after a devaluation of 33 percent on 11 January 1994, the rate is now 1 euro to 491.968 Comorian francs. The bank must keep 65 percent of its foreign currency reserves on deposit with the French Treasury. Two governments also fill its board. Under statutes signed in Paris on 22 April 2008 it had at most eight members, half named by the French government and half by the government of the Union of the Comoros, with the Governor named by the President of the Union on the finance minister's proposal; the board approved a new draft on 28 June 2024 that still awaited promulgation at the end of 2024. Under statutes in force since March 2025, France names two of the six board members, two of the four members of the banking supervision committee and two of the four members of the committee that sets monetary policy and manages reserves. The notes are printed at the Banque de France, and a new 10,000-franc note was reportedly introduced on 6 January 2026. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. It holds no gold, Mazars Fivoarana audited its 2024 accounts, and it scores 65 of 100, the highest of the 194 places with a figure.

CAYMAN ISLANDS MONETARY AUTHORITY
Cayman Islands
The Cayman Islands Monetary Authority acts as the central bank of the Cayman Islands, and the currency is the Cayman Islands dollar. In June 2015 it said it would commission an internal review of the involvement of local people and financial institutions in the FIFA corruption case, after the Caymanian businessman Jeffrey Webb was arrested in Switzerland on 27 May. The husband of its managing director Cindy Scotland, the former minister Mark Scotland, had worked for the Cayman Islands Football Association under Webb and was with Webb at the arrest; Gloria Glidden, deputy head of the authority's banking division, is the wife of the former minister Cline Glidden, who was also in Switzerland with Webb. The chairman, George McCarthy, said Scotland would remain managing director and that there was no evidence any Cayman bank had done anything wrong. That review is still under investigation. One career move runs the other way, into the authority: its own board page says director Greg Swart was managing member and chief financial officer of Farallon Capital Management LLC, a global alternative asset management firm, from 2002 to 2019, and spent about twelve years at Goldman Sachs before that, running a unit serving hedge funds and serving as president of GS Financial Products from 1991 to 1996. The page gives no dates for his board service, and taking a job is not an accusation. A commemorative 70-dollar note for the Platinum Jubilee of Queen Elizabeth II, introduced on 12 October 2023, was printed by De La Rue and is not part of the circulating series. South Korea's money is the won, issued by the Bank of Korea, which scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. One episode of government pressure is recorded. Choi Kyung-hwan became deputy prime minister for the economy and finance minister in July 2014 and pressed publicly for lower interest rates, launching a stimulus package and warning that the economy stood between a leap forward and a recession; he said in public that he had not mentioned the base rate and that the central bank should get the hint. On 14 August 2014 the bank cut its base rate by a quarter point to 2.25 percent, the first move in fifteen months, and cut again to 2.0 percent on 15 October. Reporting at the time described both cuts as made under government pressure rather than as the start of a policy cycle, and a Reuters survey ahead of the August meeting recorded a sharp reversal in market expectations that raised questions about the bank's independence. Governor Lee Ju-yeol said the decision was his committee's and that its independence was guaranteed. Independence is written into the Bank of Korea Act, but the same reporting noted a long record of governments pressing the bank to cooperate: the May 2013 cut under a previous governor was read the same way, and in October 2010 a vice finance minister attended a rate-setting meeting to deliver the government's view of the economy. Two cases are recorded, both ending in conviction. Between 2022 and 2023 a currency-exchange employee at the bank's Daejeon Sejong-Chungnam headquarters broke the rule that older coins leave the vault first, at a coin collector's request, letting 240,000 one-hundred-won coins from 2018 and 2019 go out ahead of 2017 coins; the collector made about 180 million won selling them and gave the employee about 55 million, and the Daejeon District Court imposed two years and six months in prison, a fine and confiscation. CENTRAL BANK OF MALTA
Malta
Malta uses the euro, so its interest rates are set by the European Central Bank, in which the Central Bank of Malta takes part. Its books have been checked from outside by two firms: KPMG under an approved term covering the financial years 2019 to 2025, and Deloitte Audit Ltd under a term covering 2023 to 2027. Its own case concerns governor Scicluna, a former finance minister: on 29 May 2024 he pleaded not guilty to fraud over the government's handling of a private hospital contract, the Vitals concession, while he was minister. He stepped aside in July 2024 and was reinstated in July 2025 after the European Central Bank was consulted and raised no objections; the charges remain unproven. Two findings sit at the European Central Bank: the European Union's complaints office found maladministration over president Mario Draghi's membership of the Group of Thirty, a club of central bankers and private bankers, and recommended in January 2018 that he suspend it, which the bank declined and he did not; and a speech of 18 May 2015 to a private London event was published only the next day. Malta's own share of the European Central Bank's US dollar pooled reserves is not run from Malta: the Central Bank of Ireland has managed it since 1 January 2008, at Malta's own request. Each euro-area country transferred foreign reserves to the ECB in proportion to its shareholding, and the ECB's page says those reserves are managed in a decentralised way by the national central banks, which act for the ECB on a disclosed agency basis; Malta is the one that handed the job to another country's central bank. The combined value of Ireland's and Malta's share of the ECB's US dollar pooled reserves is USD 1.5 billion, and Ireland's own portion of the ECB reserves amounted to EUR 0.4 billion. A circulating 500-pound note, part of the series that dropped two zeros from the pound, is printed by Goznak, the Russian state currency works. NATIONAL BANK OF TAJIKISTAN
Tajikistan
The National Bank of Tajikistan issues the somoni, which it keeps within a band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar. One case is recorded, as an official finding: in March 2008 the International Monetary Fund's Executive Board found the bank had supplied inaccurate information on the cotton sector, international reserves, net domestic assets and credit policy, reporting reserves of about 450 million US dollars when they were roughly a third of that and concealing that reserves were pledged as collateral for cotton loans; Tajikistan was required to repay 47.4 million US dollars. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency: 3 billion yuan with China, signed on 3 September 2015 to run three years and extendable by agreement, drawn on for 1 million yuan in January 2016; whether it is in force is not known. Its commemorative 100-somoni note, circulated on 30 October 2025, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient of Germany, that note alone and not the regular series. Its books are checked from outside by RSM Tajikistan LLC of Dushanbe, whose managing partner signed the independent auditor's report on the 2023 financial statements. Worth noticing is that the firm holds a licence to audit banks issued by the National Bank itself, so the body being audited also licenses its auditor. Mauritania
The Central Bank of Mauritania issues Mauritania's money, the ouguiya, and scores 30 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. One case is recorded, from 2020 and 2021, and it is still an investigation. In July 2020 police working under the Nouakchott-Ouest prosecutor arrested six people, one of them a bank employee, over foreign currency taken from the central bank. Early reports put the amount at about 1 million US dollars and later reports at 2.4 million, plus 500,000 dollars in counterfeit notes. By March 2021 seven people were in pretrial detention, presumed to have taken about 1 million dollars, and supporters held a sit-in demanding a quick trial. No trial or verdict is reported. The governor also signed an agreement with the World Bank treasury for advice on managing reserves. p:UGA.box:
BANK OF UGANDA
Uganda
The Bank of Uganda issues the Ugandan shilling, and the Auditor General audits its accounts. It scores 34 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption in the country. On paper it is among the less independent central banks, scoring 0.467 of 1 on a 42-rule measure of independence written into law. One case is recorded. A confidential 2018 Auditor General report to parliament said bank managers, including governor Mutebile, acted without guidelines, regulations or policies and may have intentionally neglected aspects of the closure and sale of at least seven commercial banks, including Crane Bank in 2016 and 2017. These are the findings of a report, not court verdicts. Sudhir Ruparelia, dfcu Bank and Nile River Acquisition Company are named in the case, the last two as having received money, favours or contracts from the central bank. Parliament then put the bank through a public inquiry over the same closures. The Auditor General, John Muwanga, presented his special audit to the Speaker of Parliament on 27 August 2018; it had been requested by the chairman of Parliament's Committee on Commissions, Statutory Authorities and State Enterprises the previous November, and the bank had tried to stop it. The committee, chaired by Abdu Katuntu, took evidence from the governor, Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, his deputy Louis Kasekende and other officials from late 2018 into 2019. On 1 November 2018 Katuntu sent the governor and deputy governor away for arriving without the documents on the closures. Mutebile told the committee on 12 November that the seven banks were put under resolution largely because they were insolvent, said he had never delegated his powers to agree the sale of Global Trust Bank to DFCU Bank, and said liquidation reports had been kept from him by junior staff, which raised the question in public of whether he was in charge of his own institution; he also acknowledged that the inquiry had exposed problems at the bank. The committee's report, finalised in February 2019, recommended individual accountability for the officials implicated. Demands in Parliament for action against them later stalled. On 27 August 2018 the Auditor General, John Muwanga, presented to the Speaker of Parliament a special audit of the Bank of Uganda's closure of seven commercial banks between 1993 and 2017 - Teefe Trust Bank, International Credit Bank, Greenland Bank, Co-operative Bank, National Bank of Commerce, Global Trust Bank and Crane Bank. He also acknowledged that the inquiry had exposed problems at the bank. CENTRAL BANK OF IRAQ
Iraq
The Central Bank of Iraq issues the dinar and keeps it within a band of 2 percent or less against the US dollar. It scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and 0.733 of 1 for the independence written into its law, where 1 means the bank holds the power and 0 the government. In 2012 Iraq's Board of Supreme Audit examined the bank's daily auctions of dollars to banks and found that most transactions rested on fraudulent paperwork; the country's top auditor told US officials that up to 800 million dollars a week was leaving Iraq illegally, as reported by the US Special Inspector General for Iraq Reconstruction. In October 2012 the cabinet removed governor Sinan al-Shabibi and named a successor while a parliamentary committee was examining possible manipulation of the dinar and charging that bank officials were abusing the dollar sales. A committee member said arrest warrants had been issued for 30 people, including al-Shabibi and his deputy Mudher Saleh, and the Supreme Judicial Council confirmed warrants without saying what the charges were. No court outcome was ever found, so nothing was proven; he died on 8 January 2022, and the bank mourned him as a distinguished former governor. BANK OF ISRAEL
Israel
Israel's money is the shekel and its central bank is the Bank of Israel. It scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and no government pressure was reported between 2010 and 2018. Ministerial pressure came later. Through 2025 finance minister Bezalel Smotrich publicly pressed governor Amir Yaron to cut interest rates, calling the decision to hold the rate at 4 percent wrong and asking him to reverse it, and on 4 September 2025 telling business leaders that if the governor would not lower rates he would lower taxes instead. The bank answered that the governor and the Monetary Committee decide on professional grounds alone; Smotrich said in the same remarks that the bank's independence was critical and that he had no intention of interfering. On 29 April 2002 State Comptroller Eliezer Goldberg reported that former governor Jacob Frenkel unlawfully received hundreds of thousands of shekels when he resigned, approved by a senior official who reported to him; Goldberg did not say whether the money should be demanded back. A comptroller report on 17 October 2012 found supervision of the bank's reserves dealing deficient as those reserves grew from 28 to 75 billion dollars; the bank said some issues had been corrected during the audit. Frenkel, governor from 1991 to 2000, came from the International Monetary Fund and later chaired Merrill Lynch International; he sits in the Group of Thirty alongside private-sector members such as Jane Fraser of Citi and Philipp Hildebrand of BlackRock. Stanley Fischer, governor from 2005 to 2013, came from the World Bank, the IMF and Citigroup. The bank is also one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements.

Speaking to business leaders on 4 September 2025, Smotrich said Yaron "should have lowered interest rates six months ago" and told them: "If the governor doesn't lower interest rates, I will lower taxes" - that is, he would offset the bank's monetary policy with fiscal policy of his own. The same campaign ran through earlier decisions: after the committee held the rate at 4 percent in February 2025 he called the decision wrong, said no inflationary risk justified such restrictive policy and publicly called on the governor to reverse it; after the January 2025 cut he said it should have come six months earlier and should have been deeper. The Bank of Israel answered that the governor and the Monetary Committee decide on professional grounds alone, that high inflation hurts weaker households most, and that keeping it in check is essential. Smotrich also said in the same remarks that the independence of Yaron and of the bank was critical, that he had no intention of interfering, and that monetary policy was the governor's responsibility while fiscal policy was his - so this is open ministerial pressure on rate decisions, not an attempt to change the bank's powers. p:ISR.current_paragraph: Israel's money is the shekel and its central bank is the Bank of Israel. It scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and no government pressure was reported between 2010 and 2018. Ministerial pressure came later. Through 2025 finance minister Bezalel Smotrich publicly pressed governor Amir Yaron to cut interest rates, calling the decision to hold the rate at 4 percent wrong and asking him to reverse it, and on 4 September 2025 telling business leaders that if the governor would not lower rates he would lower taxes instead. The bank answered that the governor and the Monetary Committee decide on professional grounds alone; Smotrich said in the same remarks that the bank's independence was critical and that he had no intention of interfering. On 29 April 2002 State Comptroller Eliezer Goldberg reported that former governor Jacob Frenkel unlawfully received hundreds of thousands of shekels when he resigned, approved by a senior official who reported to him; Goldberg did not say whether the money should be demanded back. On 3 February 2009 Globes reported that a draft comptroller report alleged flaws in the bank's supervision of Bank Hapoalim's sub-prime investments, on which Hapoalim wrote off 1.5 billion dollars; the bank said it had responses to all the points, and this is unproven. A comptroller report on 17 October 2012 found supervision of the bank's reserves dealing deficient as those reserves grew from 28 to 75 billion dollars; the bank said some issues had been corrected during the audit. Frenkel, governor from 1991 to 2000, came from the International Monetary Fund and later chaired Merrill Lynch International; he sits in the Group of Thirty alongside private-sector members such as Jane Fraser of Citi and Philipp Hildebrand of BlackRock. Stanley Fischer, governor from 2005 to 2013, came from the World Bank, the IMF and Citigroup. The bank is also one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements.
